author: kevaundray
content:
What I suggested in the past was to keep the BLS evidence for at least the amount of time it would take for that stake to be exited.

I believe <@520034910149410861>  had an alternative solution that relied on social slashing (I don't remember it entirely)

author: kevaundray
content: small note: keeping the BLS evidence is safe as long as we do the fork before we are under attack, ie it doesn't work in an emergency

author: tcoratger
content:
I think that the simplest solution is indeed to keep the funds blocked and keep BLS for a while. So at the PQ fork, the non-PQ validator leaves the network but we still have his ETH blocked for security reasons and we continue to accept BLS slashing proofs about votes from before the fork. This is very simple but this means that BLS is still secure at this moment (just after the fork).

Otherwise what we can also maybe do is to have a STARK to replace the BLS verification at this moment. So in this case we also keep the ETH for a while and the PQ protocol verifies a STARK proof attesting that the legacy BLS signatures are valid and constitute an infraction. This is more complex but PQ safe after the fork.

author: kevaundray
content: Actually <@363800010518822915> I was thinking of the more general case where a validator votes just before the fork with BLS and then after the fork they equivocate with their PQ public key

author: kevaundray
content: A simpler solution would be to say that at the PQ hardfork, that block is canonical. So any equivocations with BLS are just ignored (they can't do anything)

author: tcoratger
content: But making the fork block canonical doesn't solve the slashing problem, right? A validator who actually performed a double BLS vote before the fork could still evade their penalty if the decision is made to ignore all past infractions.

author: kevaundray
content: Yeah for the simpler solution, we would not penalise the equivocator, we would just ignore their equivocation

author: terencechain
content:
<@427491045308235776> <@923866336382316594> 
im not sure about “a simpler solution would be to say that at the PQ hardfork, that block is canonical.” that could also give it extra reorg power, which may be dangerous and have unintended implications

im also not sure about keeping BLS slashings post PQ fork, because if BLS is broken by then, honest validators can get slashed by forged BLS attestations. that seems worse

i think the current spec may be the best we can do given the tradeoffs. ill continue thinking about this and come back

author: tcoratger
content: What do you think about the STARK proof? Too complex maybe? But the good news is that we could reuse leanVM for this with just an additional small program in it to deal with this case.

author: terencechain
content:
Not sure. I haven't thought about that.. 
Maybe we should separate "planned" migration from "emergency" migration. for a planned migration, assuming BLS is secure through the transition, we could keep a bounded legacy slashing window. for an emergency migration, where BLS is broken, we’d reject new BLS slashing but could still delay withdrawal to leave some time for social slashing if comes to that
I think in all cases, non-PQ validators should keep the normal withdrawal delay at the transition. i don’t see a reason not to do this, it deters bad behavior close to the fork
